introduction.sentence: RNA plays an essential role in a wide variety of fundamental cellular processes, such as transcription, replication, protein synthesis and regulation of gene expression (; ).
introduction.label: ACTIVE

introduction.sentence: The structure of an RNA, including secondary structure and tertiary structure, determines its translation and other functions.
introduction.label: ACTIVE

introduction.sentence: Identifying secondary structure is a key groundwork to know ter- tiary structure and a vital premise to understand the detailed mech- anism of various biological activities, such as protein–RNA interactions and translation process.
introduction.label: ACTIVE

introduction.sentence: Therefore, there is a critical need to identify the RNA secondary structure by an unbiased and systematic manner.
introduction.label: ACTIVE

introduction.sentence: While RNA secondary structure can be obtained from a small number of RNA tertiary structures experimentally determined by low-throughput techniques such as nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), X-ray crystallography and Cryo-electron microscopy, re- cently a few experimental techniques have been developed to per- form high-throughput profiling of the RNA structure by exploiting biochemical reactions.
introduction.label: PASSIVE

introduction.sentence: For example, parallel analysis of RNA struc- ture (PARS) distinguishes double- and single-stranded regions using catalytic activities of two enzymes, RNase V1 and S1 (able to cut double-stranded and single-stranded nucleotides, respectively).
introduction.label: ACTIVE

introduction.sentence: This technique has been successfully applied to the yeast and human genomes (; ).
introduction.label: PASSIVE

introduction.sentence: Fragmentation sequencing (FragSeq), using nuclease P1 to generate fragments, was V C The Author(s) 2020.
introduction.label: ACTIVE

introduction.sentence: Published by Oxford University Press.
introduction.label: ACTIVE

introduction.sentence: For permissions, please e-mail: journals.permissions@oup.com 4576 Bioinformatics, 36(17), 2020, 4576–4582 doi: 10.1093/bioinformatics/btaa534 Advance Access Publication Date: 28 May 2020 Original Paper Downloaded from academic.oup.com/bioinformatics/article/36/17/4576/5848407 by Georgia Institute of Technology user on 13 November 2026 applied to determine single-stranded RNA regions in multiple ncRNAs.
introduction.label: ACTIVE

introduction.sentence: Besides, selective 20-hydroxyl acylation analyzed by primer extension sequencing (SHAPE-Seq) was able to measure the structures of a complex pool of RNAs but the output was found to be sensitive to noises.
introduction.label: PASSIVE

introduction.sentence: Another technique based on in vivo modification with dimethyl sulfate (DMS), which only reacts to ad- enine and cytosine, are of high quality, but DMS experiments are not included here because not all the nucleotide states are provided (; ).
introduction.label: PASSIVE

introduction.sentence: Recently, two orthogonal high-throughput sequencing-based techniques, icSHAPE (in vivo click selective 2-hydroxyl acylation and profiling experiment) and PARIS (psoralen analysis of RNA interactions and structures), have been applied to the Zika virus (Zikv) for an accurate estimate of genome-wide secondary structure profile.
introduction.label: PASSIVE

introduction.sentence: However, high-throughput genomic experiments always have high noises and are hard to cover all nucleotides on the RNA due to limited sequencing coverages (; ).
introduction.label: ACTIVE

introduction.sentence: Moreover, the sequencing experiments are of heavy experi- mental work and high costs.
introduction.label: ACTIVE

introduction.sentence: Therefore, computational methods are often required.
introduction.label: PASSIVE

introduction.sentence: Many tools have been developed to obtain locally stable secondary structure by minimizing the free energy, such as ViennaRNA (; ).
introduction.label: PASSIVE

introduction.sentence: Nonetheless, these methods are not accurate enough due to a lack of a precise free energy criterion, and the searching of the global minima is an NP-hard problem.
introduction.label: ACTIVE

introduction.sentence: To be even worse, the secondary structure with the lowest free energy is not always the actual one (Hofacker, 2014; Seetin and Mathews, 2012; ).
introduction.label: ACTIVE

introduction.sentence: Recently, with the accu- mulation of experimental genomic data, a CROSS method was developed to predict RNA secondary structural profile by a shallow artificial neural network with only one hidden layer.
introduction.label: PASSIVE

introduction.sentence: The neural network is well known to have strong self- learning and non-linear fitting ability, but it is easy to fall into local optimal solution and has slow convergence with small training data (Jin-Yue and Bao-Ling, 2012; Roberts, 2003).
introduction.label: ACTIVE

introduction.sentence: Recently, the eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) technique was proposed by aggregating multiple weak learners to obtain a combined and strong learner.
introduction.label: PASSIVE

introduction.sentence: Meanwhile, as a kind of gradient boosting model, its implementa- tion of parallel processing enables a fast model training compared to many traditional models, and can be deployed to high-performance platform for large-scale parallel computing.
introduction.label: PASSIVE

introduction.sentence: The technique was found to outperform other machine learning and deep learning tech- niques in many competitions, such as Kaggle and KDDCup (Chen and Guestrin, 2016; ), especially for datasets with sparse matrices.
introduction.label: PASSIVE

introduction.sentence: It has been successfully applied in many bio- informatic studies, such as miRNA–disease association, protein translocation, protein–protein interactions, and DNA methylation.
introduction.label: PASSIVE

introduction.sentence: In this study, we developed a new method for end-to-end predic- tion of the genome-wide RNA secondary structure profile (GRASP) from RNA sequence by using the XGBoost technique.
introduction.label: ACTIVE

introduction.sentence: The method achieves area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values of >0.9 by cross-validations on three different datasets (high-throughput PARS-Yeast and human datasets and high-quality dataset from NMR/X-ray structures), and AUC of 0.888 on another independent test of the Zikv dataset.
introduction.label: ACTIVE

introduction.sentence: The comparisons showed that our method consistently outperforms the CROSS method trained by using the shallow neural network.
introduction.label: ACTIVE

introduction.sentence: Moreover, the predictive power of our model was also supported by a correlation between predicted structure profile and minor allele frequencies (MAF) of genetic var- iants, as well as the finding that both ends of coding regions have less structures.
introduction.label: PASSIVE

methods.sentence: 2.1 Datasets For validation of our method, we employed three training datasets (PARS-Yeast, PARS-Human and SS-PDB) as also used in the previ- ous study.
methods.label: ACTIVE

methods.sentence: Since their training and test sets were not available, we followed the same steps as reported in the study to generate the datasets.
methods.label: ACTIVE

methods.sentence: In addition, another independent test set was compiled from the recently released Zikv genomic data.
methods.label: PASSIVE

methods.sentence: shows the details of three training datasets and the independent test set.
methods.label: ACTIVE

methods.sentence: The PARS-Yeast and PARS-Human datasets were derived from the experimentally measured RNA structural profiles probed by the PARS technique on the S. cerevisiae and
methods.label: PASSIVE

methods.sentence: The experimental data contain around 3200 and more than 35 000 non-redundant transcripts, respectively.
methods.label: ACTIVE

methods.sentence: In these two datasets, the ratio between double- and single-stranded frequencies was calculated as a score (PARS score) for each nucleotide.
methods.label: PASSIVE

methods.sentence: In order to obtain nucleotides with the most reliable measurements, we selected nucleotides with the highest scores on each transcript as double-stranded nucleotides (positives), and the same number with the lowest scores as the single-stranded nucleotides (negatives).
methods.label: ACTIVE

methods.sentence: Around the selected nucleo- tides, fragments were prepared to include 18 nucleotides from its up- stream and downstream, leading to a length of 37 for each sample.
methods.label: ACTIVE

methods.sentence: As fragments from different positions or transcripts might have the same sequences but different scores or labels, we kept one represen- tative fragment set as the consistent state of secondary structure if more than 90% of the fragments were in the same state, single- or double-stranded, otherwise the fragments were all removed.
methods.label: PASSIVE

methods.sentence: Here, we selected top and bottom five nucleotides in each transcript for S.cerevisiae and two for Homo sapiens in order to keep close num- bers for two species.
methods.label: ACTIVE

methods.sentence: Finally, we obtained 15 341 positives (each rep- resented by a fragment) and 15 340 negatives for the S.cerevisiae, and 29 454 positives and 31 720 negatives for the Homo sapiens, namely PARS-Yeast and PARS-Human.
methods.label: ACTIVE

methods.sentence: SS-PDB: We downloaded 1341 secondary structures of RNA from the RNAstrand, a curated database from the three-dimensional structures of RNA that were determined by X-ray or NMR and deposited in the Protein Data Bank (PDB).
methods.label: PASSIVE

methods.sentence: By removing redundant sequences with sequence identity >75% calcu- lated by CD-hit, 202 sequences remained.
methods.label: ACTIVE

methods.sentence: The sequences include totally 46 694 nucleotides, with 30 680 posi- tives (double stranded) and 16 014 negatives (single stranded), namely SS-PDB.
methods.label: ACTIVE

methods.sentence: We downloaded the experimental scores of secondary structure profiles for Zikv from the previous study.
methods.label: ACTIVE

methods.sentence: As suggested by the previous study, we selected nucleotides with raw score of 0 and 1 as double and single stranded,.

methods.sentence: 2.2 Features extraction and encoding of RNA sequences We employed a window-based strategy for feature extraction of sec- ondary structure status.
methods.label: ACTIVE

methods.sentence: For a given nucleotide, d nucleotides in the upstream and downstream were selected for its features.
methods.label: PASSIVE

methods.sentence: Here, we defined a window size l, where l ¼ 2d þ 1, and thus the window size decided the number of features to represent the nucleotide.
methods.label: ACTIVE

methods.sentence: At the beginning or end of the sequence, it was padded with the letter N if the length of upstream or downstream was less than d. After feature extraction, each nucleotide was encoded with the one-hot notation : A ¼ (1, 0, 0, 0), C ¼ (0, 1, 0, 0), G ¼ (0, 0, 1, 0), U ¼ (0, 0, 0, 1) and N ¼ (0, 0, 0, 0).
methods.label: PASSIVE

methods.sentence: Thus, the prediction of each nucleotide has an input of 4  l matrix.
methods.label: ACTIVE

methods.sentence: By testing different window sizes, we finally chosen l ¼ 37 for a balance of performance and training time.
methods.label: ACTIVE

methods.sentence: 2.3 Training of GRASP GRASP was trained by using XGBoost, which is an ensemble method to generate k Classification and Regression Trees (CART).
methods.label: PASSIVE

methods.sentence: The input of the CART includes a vector with size of 4l that is flat- tened from the feature matrix (4  l).
methods.label: PASSIVE

methods.sentence: The training procedure of XGBoost can be outlined as follows:
methods.label: PASSIVE

methods.sentence: 1. Sort values in each feature and scan the best splitting point, the values that gives the lowest gain; 2.
methods.label: ACTIVE

methods.sentence: Select the feature with the best splitting point that optimizes the objective function; 3. Repeat the splitting in the above two steps until the maximum tree depth (set hyper-parameter) is reached;
methods.label: PASSIVE

methods.sentence: 4. Make assignment to the leaves with prediction score and prune the nodes with negative gains according to a bottom-up order; 5.
methods.label: ACTIVE

methods.sentence: Continue repeating the above steps for k times (k trees); We used the implementation provided in the XGBoost Python li-
methods.label: ACTIVE

methods.sentence: brary that was optimized for distributed systems.
methods.label: PASSIVE

methods.sentence: Here, we selected l ¼ 37 after comparison (explain in detail in Section 3).
methods.label: ACTIVE

methods.sentence: We used grid search in Scikit-learn framework to find the optimal parameters.
methods.label: ACTIVE

methods.sentence: The range of parameters set up in the training process is shown in.
methods.label: PASSIVE

methods.sentence: Moreover, the optimized XGBoost models were trained on a 16 core CPU to speed up the learning process.
methods.label: PASSIVE

methods.sentence: Parameter optimization and evaluation of the models were performed using the 5-fold cross-validation.
methods.label: PASSIVE

methods.label: ACTIVE

methods.sentence: First, the in- dividual features extracted from RNA sequence were encoded and flatten.
methods.label: PASSIVE

methods.sentence: Then the models were parallelly trained by grid searching strategy with 5-fold cross-validation.
methods.label: PASSIVE

methods.sentence: The sub-model with the best AUC in validation was selected.
methods.label: PASSIVE

methods.sentence: Finally, the independent test was performed by the remained two datasets not involved in the training.
methods.label: PASSIVE

methods.sentence: The performance of the model was measured by the area under the AUC curve, accuracy (ACC), precision, recall value and F1-Score score.

methods.sentence: The 1000 Genome dataset The 1000 Genomes Phase 3 VCF file was downloaded from the Ensembl annotated by ANNOVAR, which leads to single-nucleotide variations (SNVs) along with their MAF, including 223 693 cases in 50 untranslated regions (UTR), 899 976 in 30 UTR, 16 847 in stop-gain mutations, 704 643 non-synonymous and 427 077 synonymous mutations.
methods.label: PASSIVE

methods.sentence: MAF is the frequency of the least com- mon allele in a population.
methods.label: ACTIVE

methods.sentence: For each category, SNVs were sorted and equally separated into 50 bins according to the predicted scores of secondary structure (or predicted ASA, accessible surface area, by RNA-snap) at their mutated positions.
methods.label: PASSIVE

methods.sentence: Log (Predicted values) and log (MAF) were averaged, as well as Pearson’s correlation coeffi- cients (PCC) were calculated based on the average values..

methods.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: 3.1 Prediction of RNA secondary structure profile As shown in, our method achieved AUC values of 0.942, 0.967, and 0.901 by the 5-fold cross-validation on the PARS- Human, PARS-Yeast, and SS-PDB, respectively.
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: At a threshold of 0.5, the respective accuracy values are 0.871, 0.901, and 0.844 for the prediction of secondary structure profile (nucleotides to be paired or not).
results.label: PASSIVE

results.sentence: The balanced measures by F1-score are all above 0.85, where the precision and recall values are all above 0.86.
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: In order to make stricter tests, we performed the cross-tests be- tween three datasets, where model was trained on one dataset, and tested on the other two datasets.
results.label: PASSIVE

results.sentence: As shown in, the model trained by the PARS-Human achieved an AUC essentially the same as the one achieved on the PARS-Yeast by 5-fold cross-validation (0.94 versus 0.94).
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: Meanwhile, a close AUC value was also achieved on the model trained by the PARS-Yeast (0.93 versus 0.97).
results.label: PASSIVE

results.sentence: The similar performance by the self-tests and cross-tests on the PARS- Human and PARS-Yeast demonstrated the robustness of our method on different genomes.
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: Differently, when these two models were applied to the SS-PDB dataset, the models trained by PARS- Human and PARS-Yeast achieved close but significantly lower AUC values (0.65 and 0.63).
results.label: PASSIVE

results.sentence: This is likely due to the difference in two ex- perimental techniques.
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: On the other hand, the analytical method, RNAplfold achieved lower AUC values with 0.76, 0.86, and 0.67 for PARS-Human, PARS-Yeast, and SS-PDB, respectively .
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: Notably, for PARS-Human, when we selected top and bottom five nucleotides instead of two as mentioned in the dataset, the results were similar (Supplementary Tables S3 and S4).
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: When compared with the reported results by the CROSS, a method trained by a shallow neural network, our method performs consistently better in all cross-tests datasets: the AUCs achieved by our method are 4.4~10% better than those by CROSS with an aver- age of 6.7% (Supplementary Table S2).
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: The differences in datasets should have little impact, as the improvements are essentially the same as the one (5.7%) in the independent test on the SS-ZIKV data- set by using CROSS’s online server (see Section 3.3).
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: Our method achieved slightly lower AUCs in the self-tests (the results of cross- validation).
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: 3.2 Performance of consensus model Since three training datasets represent different genomes or experi- mental techniques, it is interesting to know the performance by com- bining all datasets.
results.label: ACTIVE

results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: The remaining 10% of the three datasets were used as independent test sets.
results.label: PASSIVE

results.sentence: As shown in the, the consensus model achieved close to the highest AUC values among three independents.
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: The average AUC is 0.927, significantly higher than the 0.846, 0.840 and 0.812 by models trained only on the PARS-Human, PARS-Yeast and SS- PDB training sets, respectively.
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: Besides, it is important to note that, for the test set of SS-PDB data, the consensus model outperforms models only trained on human or yeast data with increase of AUC from less than 0.65 to nearly 0.90.
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: These improvements indicate that the consensus model could eliminate the difference between two experimental techniques and is better for general prediction of RNA secondary structures.

results.sentence: 3.4 Relation of predicted secondary structure with the MAF of genetic variants To demonstrate the biological significance of our predicted second- ary structure profiles, we examined whether the predicted paired states of nucleotides were related with the MAF of genetic variants observed from the 1000 Genomes Project for healthy individuals.
results.label: PASSIVE

results.sentence: As shown in, the unpaired probabilities (i.e. 1  paired probability) predicted by GRASP showed high correlations with MAF for most types of mutations, with the highest PCC of 0.901 from synonymous mutations.
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: This is probably because syn- onymous mutations that do not change expressed proteins affect biological functions mainly through the change of RNA secondary structure.
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: The correlation is especially clear for the paired states (left region in ) as mutations of paired nucleotides mostly destroy the paired states and likely cause diseases.
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: Relatively, the points close to 0 (unpaired states) are less related as mutations of unpaired nucleotides are less probable to change the paired states.
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: This was confirmed by the PCC of 0.925 when using the unpaired probabil- ities through mutated sequences.
results.label: PASSIVE

results.sentence: When using the changes of the un- paired probabilities, there is still a strong negative correlation, but the correlation is slightly weaker (PCC ¼ 0.853).
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: This is consistent with our previous findings that the prediction of overall states is still limited to reflecting the differences by mutations (Chen et al., 2019a; ).
results.label: PASSIVE

results.sentence: The predictions by RNAplfold achieved a PCC of 0.794 that is greater than the 0.473 by the predicted ASA (accessible surface area) from the RNAsnap-seq, agreeing with the previous study.
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: This ranking order is consistent with most types of mutations, non-synonymous mutations, stop- gain mutations, and mutations occurring in the 30 UTR ( and Supplementary Figs S1–S3).
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: 3.5 Predicted secondary structure plays as a key signal in translation To further explore the potential function of the secondary structure in translation process, we explored the distribution of paired prob- ability in coding area of mRNAs.
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: As shown in, the paired probability predicted by GRASP reveals a three-nucleotide period- icity across coding regions.
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: In each codon, the first nucleotide is al- ways the least structured and the second one is more structured than the other two, similar to previous observation (; ).
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: This vibration frequency indicates there is an un- ambiguous definition of codon boundaries during translation pro- cess.
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: The results of RNAplfold also shows periodicity, but not so obvious.
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: Moreover, it was shown that there was a sudden drop and then fast rise in paired probability near the start codons as well as stop codons.
results.label: PASSIVE

results.sentence: The curve of GRASP forms a deeper bottom than that of RNAplfold .
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: Namely, both the starting site and ending site tend to be unpaired.
results.label: PASSIVE

results.sentence: This is consistent with the previous finding that over 80% of the start codon are free of secondary structure by ana- lyzing mRNAs of prokaryotic and eukaryotic, as well as free energy preference at the 50 and 30 ends of siRNA.
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: This kind of enrichment of unpaired nucleotides can help to start the protein translation process.
results.label: ACTIVE

results.sentence: Additionally, the transition of secondary structure over the bound- ary is likely an important signal for a correct recognition of coding regions.
results.label: ACTIVE

discussion.sentence: In this study, we have developed a new method GRASP to predict RNA secondary structure from sequence based on XGBoost.
discussion.label: ACTIVE

discussion.sentence: To train the model, we used sequence information around a given nu- cleotide.
discussion.label: ACTIVE

discussion.sentence: We found that a window size of 37 nucleotides provided the best performance, as shown in Supplementary Table S1 and.
discussion.label: ACTIVE
